launches.title: Affinity’s creative studio is now available on iPad for free
launches.excerpt: Canva has released Affinity for iPad, bringing professional-grade tools for vector graphics, photo editing, illustration, and page layouts to Apple’s tablet device at no cost for individuals. The application is optimised for touchscreens and the Apple Pencil, supporting features such as pressure sensitivity, tilt, barrel roll, squeeze, and hover. It also includes a new Sketch Studio intended for freehand drawing and converting rough sketches into geometric shapes. Projects can be saved in a unified file format compatible with major design types to minimise the need for exporting and converting. In addition, the software integrates an AI Studio that offers generative background expansion, automated motion blur, noise reduction, and image resolution scaling. When Canva acquired Affinity developer Serif in 2024, users expressed concerns about potential shifts to subscription models and forced artificial intelligence integration, prompting a pledge that core features would remain accessible without a subscription. True to that promise, the core tools are free for individuals with a standard Canva account, while the optional AI features require a paid Canva Pro subscription starting at eighteen dollars per month.

launches.title: Ford launches a ‘privacy promise’ and explains how and why it uses customer data
launches.excerpt: Ford has introduced a public privacy promise ahead of launching a new generation of connected vehicles, including models built on its upcoming universal electric vehicle platform. The automaker has also launched a website designed to educate customers about how, where and why the company uses their data, alongside instructions on how to change related settings. Chief privacy officer Kristin Jones stated that the initiative aims to provide clarity regarding data practices and build a relationship of trust with consumers. While vehicle controls have existed for years, the company wants to communicate them more clearly in response to low consumer awareness around data collection. Recent industry controversies, such as General Motors facing a multimillion-dollar settlement over data sharing, have highlighted growing concerns about how automakers handle customer information. Ford stated that it will not share driving behavior information with data brokers or use data for targeted advertising. The new educational website explains data collection practices and guides customers through opting in or out of information sharing. Jones noted that opting out of certain data sharing will make some modern features, such as real-time navigation and built-in roadside assistance, inaccessible. Collecting data on vehicle health allows the company to provide owners with maintenance updates while supporting research and development for future technologies. Jones emphasized that the manufacturer is not trying to monetize customer data, but rather offer products and services that provide user value.

launches.title: Amazon Bedrock expands API support and introduces Cross-Region Inferencing for OpenAI models in AWS GovCloud (US)
launches.excerpt: Amazon Bedrock has introduced support for the OpenAI GPT-5.6 models, specifically Terra and Luna, on the bedrock-runtime endpoint within AWS GovCloud (US) regions. The update includes compatibility with the Responses, Converse, and Chat Completions APIs. Additionally, Amazon Web Services has added support for Cross-Region Inference for these models in AWS GovCloud (US). This feature automatically routes inference requests across multiple AWS GovCloud regions to provide higher throughput and increased redundancy. Customers can scale their usage during demand spikes while maintaining US data sovereignty without having to manually manage capacity across multiple regions. Because these native OpenAI APIs operate on the bedrock-runtime endpoint, they integrate with existing account-level controls used for other Bedrock models. Consequently, model usage appears in Bedrock model invocation logging, which can be delivered to Amazon S3 or Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Furthermore, activity is tracked in Amazon CloudWatch metrics that cover invocation counts, token counts, latency, throttles, and errors. Spend attribution is also supported through itemised data in AWS Cost Explorer and the AWS Cost and Usage Report. Cross-Region Inference for OpenAI models is now available across all AWS regions where OpenAI models are offered on Amazon Bedrock.

launches.title: Web Search now available on Kiro in AWS GovCloud (US)
launches.excerpt: Kiro web search is now available in AWS GovCloud, providing agents with real-time access to current information on the internet. This feature allows agent answers to draw upon up-to-date search results and page content. The agent automatically triggers web searches when handling questions that involve recent developments or topics that fall outside the scope of its training data. Responses that incorporate information from web results include appropriate citations. Enterprise administrators operating in AWS GovCloud have the ability to disable web search and web fetch functions for their entire organisation directly through the Kiro console under the settings menu. Additionally, teams can remove these web tools from individual custom agents or restrict them by implementing capability-based permission rules. Further information regarding the new capability can be found within the AWS GovCloud documentation and the monitoring and tracking guide. Users can also reach out to their designated AWS account team for assistance or consult the main Kiro product page to learn more about the platform.

launches.title: Daybreak Red from OpenAI now available to eligible customers on Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US-East)
launches.excerpt: OpenAI has made its Daybreak Red security model available to eligible customers using Amazon Bedrock in the AWS GovCloud (US-East) region as well as the US East (Ohio) region. Designed as part of the broader Daybreak cyber defense initiative, the GPT-5.6 Cyber model is intended to assist authorized security teams with vulnerability research, exploit reproduction, and mitigation development. The platform is engineered to provide verified defenders with greater latitude to investigate complex security problems by featuring reduced refusal rates for sensitive tasks alongside enhanced identity verification, monitoring, and access controls. Operating on Amazon Bedrock's next-generation inference engine, the system enforces zero-operator access at the chip level to maintain data security. Furthermore, user inference data is not utilised to train models, and customers are not required to share their Daybreak Red data with OpenAI. To utilise the service, interested organisations must first enrol in Daybreak access through OpenAI and verify their eligibility by contacting OpenAI or their designated AWS account team. Once approval has been granted, customers can collaborate with their AWS account team to enable access within their environment.

geo.title: Supermarket freezers across Europe hit by second suspected cyber-attack
geo.excerpt: Supermarket chains across at least seven European countries have reported sudden overnight temperature rises in their refrigerators and freezers. Retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden confirmed they were victims of cyber-attacks impacting their refrigeration systems. The incidents closely mirror a similar attack in France last month where hackers seized control of cooling units in up to 700 supermarkets, raising temperatures to 50C and causing extensive food losses and fires. Swedish chains Coop and ICA stated that a limited number of their stores had been affected, with some locations reporting that freezers were completely destroyed. Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize confirmed that dozens of its supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were hit, forcing stores to remove fresh and frozen products from sale. Other affected groups included Carrefour Belgium, Colruyt, Intermarché and Ikea, which had to discard food items as a precaution. In Estonia, attackers accessed a computer controlling refrigeration systems at a supermarket, though the issue was addressed quickly with minimal damage. Irish chain SuperValu reported that 13 of its stores were impacted by a cyber-incident affecting a specific refrigeration model. Cybersecurity experts noted that the attacks involved no financial demands and appeared to be acts of sabotage exploiting thousands of exposed and unpatched operational technology devices reachable via the internet.

geo.title: European supermarkets targeted in second reported cyberattack
geo.excerpt: Supermarkets across Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden reported anomalies in their freezer systems on Monday in an apparent cyberattack reminiscent of a similar incident in France three weeks prior. Swedish supermarket chains ICA and Coop stated that a limited number of their shops had been affected, with ICA looking into the scale of the issue and Coop noting that six of its roughly 800 stores were impacted. Dutch supermarket chain Ahold Delhaize reported an overnight information technology incident affecting freezers in several Belgian and Luxembourg stores, while Irish public broadcaster RTE stated that 13 supermarkets were hit. Other chains including Carrefour, Intermarche and Spar were also targeted, with a Carrefour spokesperson in Belgium confirming the event was a cyberattack. The Belgian prosecutor's office subsequently opened a criminal investigation into the disruption. European Commissioner for Agriculture and Food Christophe Hansen described the attacks as a deliberate attempt to disrupt Europe's food supplies, noting that while food security remained safe, the resulting food waste and impact on businesses were real. The incident forced stores to discard spoiled products and prompted investigations by authorities such as Sweden's National Cybersecurity Center. Officials highlighted that the disruption involved exposed operational technology devices, which are increasingly monitored and controlled remotely, creating new vulnerabilities for cybercriminals to exploit.

geo.title: Uganda begins withdrawing troops from Somalia after two decades
geo.excerpt: Uganda has begun withdrawing its troops from Somalia, marking the start of a phased withdrawal that will conclude by the end of 2027. Uganda originally sent troops to Somalia in 2007 as part of an African Union peacekeeping force established to support the government against Al-Shabab militants. An initial contingent of 109 Ugandan soldiers departed from Mogadishu on Friday, with the first cohort already returning to Uganda. Around 4,500 Ugandan troops are currently stationed in Somalia under the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission, alongside another 2,000 deployed through bilateral agreements. The military stated that the complete withdrawal will allow the Somali Armed Forces to take full responsibility for national security. Meanwhile, the future of the African Union mission has faced uncertainty following the United States decision to end funding for a supporting UN logistics office. The United States, which is the coalition's largest donor, expressed frustration regarding limited progress against Al-Shabab and a perceived failure by the Somali government to implement political reforms. This announcement coincided with the conclusion of the UN political mission in Somalia, which transferred its responsibilities to the Somali government and UN agencies after more than thirty years. Somalia is scheduled to hold elections in May next year, though ongoing insecurity and opposition disputes continue to threaten the electoral process as Al-Shabab maintains control over large areas of central and southern Somalia.

invest.title: Crude oil dives to session low on Iran peace talk hopes ahead of midterms
invest.excerpt: Crude oil prices fell sharply on Monday, reaching session lows following signals from senior United States and Iranian officials that they remain open to diplomatic solutions. Brent crude futures dropped 6.4% to $106.20 a barrel by mid-morning, while United States West Texas Intermediate declined 6.5% to $97.35 per barrel. United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that President Donald Trump prefers to resolve the conflict diplomatically rather than use military force. Although Trump previously indicated he would not attack Iran before the United States midterms, energy markets had already priced in the risk of a major military escalation following the elections. Rubio noted over the weekend that the president has not yet made a final decision and retains the ability to act militarily if necessary. Simultaneously, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi indicated that an agreement with Washington is achievable if the United States demonstrates goodwill and actively seeks peace. Araghchi explained that mediators are currently discussing a proposal presented by Iran during the United Nations General Assembly in September, which entails lifting sanctions, reducing regional military presence, and removing the blockade. Conversely, Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei urged the nation's armed forces to counter any level of threat with an immediate and unrestricted response. Analysts note that ongoing attacks on shipping vessels and refineries in the Middle East suggest that broader conflict concerns will persist in the near term despite renewed diplomatic optimism.

invest.title: Stock market after midterm elections: What S&P 500 history shows
invest.excerpt: Financial markets typically experience anxiety ahead of midterm elections, but historical data shows that stocks generally perform strongly regardless of the political outcome. A CNBC analysis of S&P 500 returns from 1980 through 2024 reveals that the index averaged gains of 0.2 percent after one day and one week, and 1.1 percent after one month, across both presidential and midterm contests. One year later, the index climbed an average of 13.7 percent following midterms, with positive returns recorded in 91 percent of cases and gains following all eleven midterms between 1982 and 2022. Short-term returns proved less reliable, particularly after presidential elections, which yielded slightly negative averages over the first day and week. Analysts note that markets often prefer a divided government, registering an average one-year increase of 15 percent across fifteen elections that left no single party in complete control, compared to 11.5 percent following single-party victories. Despite these historical trends, broader economic drivers such as Federal Reserve policy, corporate earnings cycles, artificial intelligence developments, and global geopolitics ultimately carry more weight for market performance than election results alone.
